¶

'''witheringly''' (wiᴛ̵ʜ′ėr-ing-li), ''adv.'' In a manner tending to wither or cause to shrink.
{{smaller block|<poem>But we must wander ''witheringly'',
In other lands to die.</poem>
{{right|''Byron'', Hebrew Melodies, The Wild Gazelle.}}}}

'''witherite''' (wiᴛ̵ʜ′ėr-īt), ''n.'' [Named by Werner after W. ''Withering'', an English medical practitioner and scientist (1741–99), who, in 1784, published an analysis and description of a specimen of this mineral obtained from a lead-mine at Alston Moor in Cumberland, England.] Native barium carbonate. {{smaller|It occurs crystallized, also columnar or granular massive, and has a white, gray, or yellow color. Also called ''barolite''.}}

'''witherling<sup>1</sup>†''' (wiᴛ̵ʜ′ėr-ling), ''n.'' [< ME. ''witherling''; < ''wither''<sup>1</sup> + ''-ling''<sup>1</sup>.] An opponent, enemy, or adversary.
{{smaller block|<poem>Grete wel the gode
Quen Godild my moder,
And sey that hethene king,
Thû cristes ''witherling'',
that iche lef and dere
On londe am riued here.</poem>
{{right|''King Horn'', l. 156.}}}}

'''witherling<sup>2</sup>†''' (wiᴛ̵ʜ′ėr-ling), ''n.'' [< ''wither''<sup>2</sup> + ''-ling''<sup>1</sup>.] One who or that which is withered or decrepit.
{{smaller block|All these braunches of heretikes fallen from the church, the vine of Christes misticall body, seme thei neuer so freshe & grene, bee yet in dede but ''witherlinges''.
{{right|''Sir T. More'', Works, p. 186.}}}}

'''withernam''' (wiᴛ̵ʜ′ėr-nam), ''n.'' [< ME. *''withernam'', < AS. ''withernām'' (= G. ''widernahme''), re-

raw_text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|wither|6954|within}}</noinclude>erally: as, to ''wither'' a person by a look or glance; reputations ''withered'' by scandal.
{{smaller block|<poem>The treacherous air
Of absence ''withers'' what was once so fair.</poem>
{{right|''Wordsworth'', Sonnets, iii. 25.}}}}
{{smaller block|He ''withers'' marrow and mind.
{{right|''Tennyson'', Ancient Sage.}}}}

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' '''1.''' To lose the sap or juice; dry and shrivel up; lose freshness and bloom; fade.
{{smaller block|Shall he not pull up the roots thereof, and cut off the fruit thereof, that it ''wither''? it shall ''wither'' in all the leaves of her spring. {{right|Ezek. xvii. 9.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Leaves have their time to fall,
And flowers to ''wither'' at the north wind’s breath.</poem>
{{right|''Mrs. Hemans'', The Hour of Death.}}}}
'''2.''' To become dry and wrinkled, as from the loss or lack of animal moisture; lose pristine freshness, bloom, softness, smoothness, vigor, or the like, as from age or disease; decay.
{{smaller block|A fair face will ''wither''. ''Shak.'', Hen. V., v. 2. 170.
<poem>There, left a subject to the wind and rain,
And scorch’d by suns, it ''withers'' on the plain.</poem>
{{right|''Pope'', Iliad, iv. 559.}}}}
'''3.''' To decay generally; decline; languish; pass away.
{{smaller block|<poem>When few dayes faren were, the fre kyng Teutra
Wex welke of his wound, & ''widrit'' to dethe.</poem>
{{right|''Destruction of Troy'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 5301.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>And now I wax old,
Seke, sory, and cold,
As muk apon mold
I ''widder'' away.</poem>
{{right|''Towneley Mysteries'', p. 21.}}}}
{{smaller block|That which is of God we defend; . . . that which is otherwise, let it ''wither'' even in the root from whence it hath sprung. {{right|''Hooker'', Eccles. Polity, ii. 1.}}}}

{{smaller block|The individual ''withers'', and the world is more and more. {{right|''Tennyson'', Locksley Hall.}}}}

'''wither-.''' See ''wither''<sup>1</sup>, ''adv.''

'''wither-band''' (wiᴛ̵ʜ′ėr-band), ''n.'' A piece of iron fixed under a saddle nearly over the withers of the horse, to strengthen the bow.

'''withered<sup>1</sup>''' (wiᴛ̵ʜ′ėrd), ''p. a.'' Shriveled; faded.

'''withered<sup>2</sup>''' (wiᴛ̵ʜ′ėrd), ''a.''   [< ''wither-s'' + ''-ed''<sup>2</sup>.]   Having withers (of this or that specified kind).

{{smaller block|Some with their Manes Frizzled up, to make ’em appear high ''Wither’d'', that they look’d as Fierce as one of Hungess’s Wild Boars. {{right|Quoted in ''Ashton’s'' Social Life in Reign of Queen Anne, [II. 165.}}}}

'''witheredness''' (wiᴛ̵ʜ′ėrd-nes), ''n.'' A withered state or condition. [Rare.]

{{smaller block|Do ye complain of the dead ''witheredness'' of good affections? {{right|''Bp. Hall'', Contemplations, v. 11.}}}}

{{smaller block|Water them as soon as set, till they have recovered their ''witheredness.'' {{right|''Mortimer'', Husbandry.}}}}

'''withering''' (wiᴛ̵ʜ′ėr-ing), ''p. a.'' Blasting; blighting; scorching: as, a ''withering'' glance; a ''withering'' wind.

<poem>How many a spirit born to bless
Has sunk beneath that ''withering'' name!</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Moore'', Lalla Rookh, The Fire-Worshippers.}}}}

{{smaller block|The attacking column was under a ''withering'' fire. {{right|''The Century'', XXXVI. 250.}}}}

{{smaller block|'''Withering cancer''', scirrhous cancer in which there is a tendency to shrinkage and atrophy.}}

'''withering-floor''' (wiᴛ̵ʜ′ėr-ing-flōr), ''n.'' The drying-floor of a malt-house: according to the established arrangement, the second floor.

{{smaller block|All such [imperfect] grains are apt to become very damaging upon the ''withering floor.'' {{right|''Ure'', Dict., III. 187.}}}}

'''witheringly''' (wiᴛ̵ʜ′ėr-ing-li), ''adv.'' In a manner tending to wither or cause to shrink.
{{smaller block|<poem>But we must wander ''witheringly'',
In other lands to die.</poem>
{{right|''Byron'', Hebrew Melodies, The Wild Gazelle.}}}}

'''witherite''' (wiᴛ̵ʜ′ėr-īt), ''n.''   [Named by Werner after W. ''Withering'', an English medical practitioner and scientist (1741–99), who, in 1784, published an analysis and description of a specimen of this mineral obtained from a lead-mine at Alston Moor in Cumberland, England.]   Native barium carbonate. {{smaller|It occurs crystallized, also columnar or granular massive, and has a white, gray, or yellow color. Also called ''barolite''.}}

'''witherling<sup>1</sup>†''' (wiᴛ̵ʜ′ėr-ling), ''n.''   [< ME. ''witherling''; < ''wither''<sup>1</sup> + ''-ling''<sup>1</sup>.]   An opponent, enemy, or adversary.
{{smaller block|<poem>Grete wel the gode
Quen Godild my moder,
And sey that hethene king,
Thû cristes ''witherling'',
that iche lef and dere
On londe am riued here.</poem>
{{right|''King Horn'', l. 156.}}}}

'''witherling<sup>2</sup>†''' (wiᴛ̵ʜ′ėr-ling), ''n.''   [< ''wither''<sup>2</sup> + ''-ling''<sup>1</sup>.]   One who or that which is withered or decrepit.
{{smaller block|All these braunches of heretikes fallen from the church, the vine of Christes misticall body, seme thei neuer so freshe & grene, bee yet in dede but ''witherlinges''.
{{right|''Sir T. More'', Works, p. 186.}}}}

'''withernam''' (wiᴛ̵ʜ′ėr-nam), ''n.''   [< ME. *''withernam'', < AS. ''withernām'' (= G. ''widernahme''), retaking, reception, < ''wither'', again, + *''nām'', a taking, seizure: see ''wither''<sup>1</sup> and ''nam''<sup>2</sup>, ''name''<sup>2</sup>.]   In ''law'': (''a'') An unlawful distress, or forbidden taking, as of a thing distrained, out of the county, so that the sheriff cannot upon the replevin make deliverance thereof to the party distrained. (''b'') The reprisal of other cattle or goods, in lieu of those unjustly taken, eloigned, or otherwise withholden. The cattle or goods thus taken are said to be ''taken in withernam.'' [Now obsolete.]

'''withe-rod''' (with′rod), ''n.'' A North American shrub, ''Viburnum cassinoides'', a species formerly included in ''V. nudum.''

'''withers''' (wiᴛ̵ʜ′ėrz), ''n. pl.''   [Also ''witters''; lit. the parts that are ‘against,’ the resisting part; < ''wither''<sup>1</sup>, ''adv.'' Cf. G. ''wider-rist'', a horse’s withers, < ''wider'', against, + ''rist'', wrist, instep, also elevated part, withers.]   '''1.''' The highest part of the back of a horse, between the shoulder-blades and behind the root of the neck, where the mane ceases to grow: as, a horse 15 hands high at the ''withers.'' {{smaller|The name is extended to the same part of some other animals: as, an antelope with high ''withers''; the sacred ox, with a hump on the ''withers.'' See cut under ''horse.''}}
{{smaller block|Let the galled jade wince; our ''withers'' are unwrung.
{{right|''Shak.'', Hamlet, iii. 2. 253.}}}}
{{smaller block|Contrive that the saddle may pinch the beast in his ''withers.'' {{right|''Swift'', Advice to Servants (Groom).}}}}
'''2.''' The barbs or flukes of a harpoon; the witters: so called by British whalemen.

'''withershins''' (wiᴛ̵ʜ′ėr-shinz), ''adv.''   [Also ''widdershins, widdersinnis, widishins, widdersins'', ''wodershins'', etc.; according to a common view, lit. ‘against the sun,’ < ''wither''<sup>1</sup>, against, contrary to, + ''-shins'', ''-sins'', etc., a form of ''sun'', with adverbial gen. ''-s''. More prob. ''withershins'' is a corruption of *''witherlins'', *''witherling'', < ''wither''<sup>1</sup> + ''-ling''<sup>2</sup>.]   In the opposite direction; hence, in the wrong way. [Scotch.]
{{smaller block|Go round it three times ''widershins'', and every time say, “Open, door!” ''Child Rowland'' (Child’s Ballads, I. 248).}}
{{smaller block|<poem>And my love and his bonnie ship
Turn’d ''widdershins'' about.</poem>
{{right|''The Lowlands of Holland'' (Child’s Ballads, II. 215).}}}}

'''wither-wrung''' (wiᴛ̵ʜ′ėr-rung), ''a.''   [< ''with-er(s)'' + ''wrung''.]   Injured in the withers, as a horse.
{{smaller block|The hurt expressed by ''witherwrung'' sometimes is caused by the bite of a horse, or by a saddle being unfit.
{{right|''Farrier’s Dict.'' (''Johnson.'')}}}}

'''with-go†''' (wiᴛ̵ʜ-gō′), ''v. t.''   [< ''with-'' + ''go''.]   To forgo; give up.
{{smaller block|Esau, . . . who . . . did ''withgo'' his birthright.
{{right|''Barrow'', Sermons, III. xv.}}}}

'''withhault†''' (wiᴛ̵ʜ-hâlt′). A spurious preterit of ''withhold''. ''Spenser'', F. Q., II. xi. 9.

'''withhold''' (wiᴛ̵ʜ-hōld′), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''withheld'', ppr. ''withholding''.   [< ME. ''withholden'', ''withhalde'', keep back, hold back; < ''with-'', against, + ''hold''<sup>1</sup>, ''v.'' Cf. ''withdraw''.]   '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To hold back; keep from action; restrain; check.
{{smaller block|Enforcest thow the to aresten or ''withholden'' the swyftnesse and the sweygh of hir turnynge wheel?
{{right|''Chaucer'', Boëthius, ii. prose 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>You all did love him once, not without cause;</poem> What cause ''withholds'' you then to mourn for him?
{{right|''Shak.'', J. C., iii. 2. 108.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Life, anguish, death, immortal love,
Ceasing not, mingled, unrepress’d,
Apart from place, ''withholding'' time.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Arabian Nights.}}}}
'''2.''' To keep back; refrain from doing, giving, permitting, etc.: as, to ''withhold'' payment; to ''withhold'' assent to something.
{{smaller block|''Withhold'' revenge, dear God! ’tis not my fault.
{{right|''Shak.'', 3 Hen. VI., ii. 2. 7.}}}}
{{smaller block|Was it ever denied that the favours of the Crown were constantly bestowed and ''withheld'' purely on account of . . . religious opinions?
{{right|''Macaulay'', Sir J. Mackintosh.}}}}
'''3†.''' To keep; retain; hold; detain.
{{smaller block|It [the Lord’s Prayer] is short, for it sholde be kond the more lightly, and for to ''withholden'' it the more esily in herte. {{right|''Chaucer'', Parson’s Tale.}}}}
{{smaller block|We haue herde sey that ye ''with-holde'' alle the sowdioures that to yow will come. ''Merlin'' (E. E. T. S.), ii. 203.}}
'''4†.''' To keep; maintain.
{{smaller block|<poem>He . . . ran to London unto seynt Poules,
To seken him a chaunterie for soules,
Or with a bretherhed to been ''withholde''.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Gen. Prol. to C. T., l. 511.}}}}
'''5†.''' To engage; retain.
{{smaller block|To us surgiens aperteneth that we do to every wight the best that we kan whereas we been ''withholde''.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Tale of Melibeus.}}}}

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' To refrain; stay back; hold one’s self in check.

{{smaller block|They ''withheld'' and did no more hurte, & y<sup>e</sup> people came trembling, & brought them the best provissions they had.
{{right|''Bradford'', Plymouth Plantation, p. 104.}}}}

{{smaller block|He was fled, and so they missed of him; but understood that Squanto was alive; so they ''withheld'', and did no hurt.
{{right|''N. Morton'', New England’s Memorial, p. 71.}}}}

'''withholder''' (wiᴛ̵ʜ-hōl′dėr), ''n.''   [< ''withhold'' + ''-er''<sup>1</sup>.]   One who withholds.

{{smaller block|The words are spoken against them that invade tithes and church rights; and that which is there threatened happened to this ''withholder''.
{{right|''Stephens'', Addition to Spelman on Sacrilege, p. 138.}}}}

'''withholdment''' (wiᴛ̵ʜ-hōld′ment), ''n.''   [< ''withhold'' + ''-ment''.]   The act of withholding. ''Imp. Dict.''

'''within''' (wi-ᴛ̵ʜin′), ''adv.'' and ''prep.''   [< ME. ''within'', ''withinne'', ''withynne'', ''withinnen'', < AS. ''withinnan'', on the inside, < ''with'', against, with, + ''innan'', adv., in: see ''in''<sup>1</sup>.]   '''I.''' ''adv.'' '''1.''' In or into the interior; inside; as regards the inside; on the inside; internally.

<poem>Thai thurle a nutte, and stuffe it so ''withinne''
With brymstoon, chaf, and cedria, thees three.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Palladius'', Husbondrie (E. E. T. S.), p. 34.}}}}

{{smaller block|Damascus does not answer ''within'' to its outward appearance.
{{right|''Pococke'', Description of the East, II. i. 118.}}}}

{{smaller block|It is designed, ''within'' and without, of two stories.
{{right|''E. A. Freeman'', Venice, p. 50.}}}}

'''2.''' In the mind, heart, or soul; inwardly.

{{smaller block|You frame my thoughts, and fashion me ''within''.
{{right|''Spenser'', Sonnets, viii.}}}}

{{smaller block|I am, ''within'', thy love; without, thy master.
{{right|''T. Tomkis'' (?), Albumazar, iv. 11.}}}}

<poem>Think not the worse, my friends, I shed not tears;
Great griefs lament ''within.''</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Fletcher'', Valentinian, iv. 4.}}}}

'''3.''' In the house or dwelling; indoors; at home: as, the master is ''within.''

<poem>But at this hour the house doth keep itself;
There ’s none ''within.'' ''Shak.'', As you Like it, iv. 3. 83.</poem>

{{smaller block|''Serv.'' Your brother, sir, is speaking to a gentleman in the street, and says he knows you are ''within.''

''Joseph S.'' ’Sdeath, blockhead, I’m not ''within''—I’m out for the day.
{{right|''Sheridan'', School for Scandal, iv. 3.}}}}

'''From within''', from the inside; from the inner place or point of view.

{{smaller block|We look ''from within'', and see nothing but the mould formed by the elements in which we are incased; other observers look from without, and see us as living statues.
{{right|''O. W. Holmes'', Professor, viii.}}}}

'''II.''' ''prep.'' '''1.''' In or into the inner or interior part or parts of; inside of; in the space inclosed or bounded by: as, ''within'' the city: opposed to ''without.''

{{smaller block|Mount Syon is ''with inne'' the Cytee.
{{right|''Mandeville'', Travels, p. 92.}}}}

<poem>Come not ''within'' these doors; ''within'' this roof
The enemy of all your graces lives.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Shak.'', As you Like it, ii. 3. 17.}}}}

{{smaller block|Accominticus and Passataquack are two conuenient Harbours for small Barkes: and a good Country ''within'' their craggy clifts.
{{right|''Capt. John Smith'', Works, II. 193.}}}}

{{smaller block|And now the Kingdom is come to Unity ''within'' it self, one King and one People.
{{right|''Baker'', Chronicles, p. 78.}}}}

<poem>Without and eke ''within''
The Walls of London there is Sin.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Howell'', Letters, I. vi. 51.}}}}

{{smaller block|The perilous situation of the Christian cavaliers pent up and beleaguered ''within'' the walls of Alhama spread terror among their friends. {{right|''Irving'', Granada, p. 47.}}}}

'''2.''' Included or comprehended in.

{{smaller block|Extension apprehended is said to be ''within'' consciousness. {{right|''Veitch'', Introd. to Descartes’s Method, p. lxx.}}}}

'''3.''' Among.

{{smaller block|To save our selves therefore, and resist the common enemy, it concerns us mainly to agree ''within'' ourselves. {{right|''Milton'', True Religion.}}}}

{{smaller block|When we were come ''within'' the sandy hills, we were surprised at the sight of a magnificent tent, where a handsome collation was prepared. {{right|''Pococke'', Description of the East, I. 13.}}}}

'''4.''' In the course, range, reach, compass, or limits of; not beyond or more than: of distance, time, length, quantity. {{smaller|(''a'') Of distance: At or to a point distant less than; nearer than: as, ''within'' a mile of Edinburgh.}}

<poem>As sone as Ermones the kyng
Sawe that he was ''withynne'' his wepons length,
Anon he smote Att hym with all his strength.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Generydes'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 3044.}}}}

{{smaller block|The place shewn us for this City consisted of only a few Houses, on the tops of the Mountains, ''within'' about half a Mile of the Sea. {{right|''Maundrell'', Aleppo to Jerusalem, p. 48.}}}}

{{smaller block|Not the sage Alquife, the magician in Don Belianis of Greece, nor the no less famous Urganda the sorceress, his wife, . . . could pretend to come ''within'' a league of the truth. {{right|''Sterne'', Tristram Shandy, ii. 19.}}}}

{{smaller|(''b'') Of time: In the limits or course of; before the expiration of; in: as, he will be here ''within'' two hours.}}

<poem>Thow getis tydandis I trowe, ''within'' tene dayes,
That some trofere es tydde sene thow fro home turnede.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Morte Arthure'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 3452.}}}}<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
